questions.s: A man is brought to a THQ hospital after being dragged along a road by a motorcycle. A doctor examining his thigh notes that the superficial layer of skin has been scraped away, with tags of epidermis heaped up at one end of the injury. What does this injury most reliably indicate?
o: The exact time of the injury
questions.e: An abrasion removes the superficial epidermis, and the heaped-up tags of skin collect at the end where the force finished, so abrasions show the direction of force; they can also reproduce the pattern of the object. Sharp weapons produce incised or stab wounds, and an abrasion says nothing about deeper bone injury.

questions.s: A man was struck on the head with a heavy wooden stick. There is a 4 cm wound over the parietal bone that at first glance looks like a clean cut. On close inspection its margins are slightly bruised and crushed, and strands of tissue and hair bulbs bridge the depth of the wound. How should this wound be classified?
questions.e: Blunt force over a bone close to the skin, such as the scalp, splits the skin into a straight wound that can mimic a cut, but bruised margins and bridging strands of tissue, vessels and hair bulbs show it is a split laceration. An incised wound from a sharp edge has clean margins and no tissue bridges.

questions.s: At autopsy a firearm entry wound on the chest is surrounded by a zone of burnt hair, blackening that can be wiped away and fine punctate tattooing that cannot be wiped off. There is an abrasion collar but no muzzle imprint. What is the most likely range of fire?
questions.e: Burning, blackening (smoke) and tattooing (embedded unburnt powder grains) around an entry wound mean the muzzle was close to the skin but not touching it. In a contact wound the gases enter the wound, often with a muzzle imprint and little powder outside. Distant shots show only the abrasion collar, and exit wounds have no collar or powder marks.

questions.s: A skull recovered from a field has a round hole in the frontal bone. The outer table margin of the hole is sharp and punched-out, while the inner table is chipped away to form a crater wider on the inside. What does this defect represent?
questions.e: A bullet entering the skull punches a clean hole in the outer table and chips a wider cone from the inner table, so internal bevelling marks an entry wound. At an exit wound the bevelling is on the outer table. A hammer causes a depressed or terraced fracture, and animal damage does not produce a neat cone.

questions.s: A 22-year-old woman is found dead in a locked room. There are several shallow, parallel, superficial cuts across the front of the left wrist, and one deep cut that has severed the radial artery. Her clothing is undisturbed. What do the shallow cuts most likely represent?
questions.e: Multiple shallow, parallel cuts beside one deep wound on an accessible site such as the wrist are hesitation (tentative) cuts, typical of suicide while the person gathers resolve. Defence wounds are on the palms, fingers and the outer forearms of a victim protecting themselves. Postmortem wounds do not gape or bleed.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man is found dead with multiple stab wounds to the chest. Which additional finding most strongly suggests that the death was homicidal?
o: Cuts on the palms and fingers
Wounds on the left side of the chest
A knife lying beside the body
questions.e: Cuts on the palms, fingers and outer forearms are defence wounds sustained when a victim grabs at a blade or raises the arms, and they strongly indicate homicide. A weapon near the body is consistent with suicide, and suicides often move clothing aside before stabbing. Left-sided wounds occur in all manners of death.

questions.s: A burnt body is recovered from a house fire in Lahore. The police suspect that the man was killed elsewhere and the house set on fire to hide the crime. Which autopsy finding best shows that he was alive when the fire started?
o: Soot in the airways below the cords
questions.e: Soot in the trachea and bronchi below the vocal cords, with a raised carboxyhaemoglobin level, shows the person was breathing in the smoke and so was alive during the fire. Pugilistic attitude, heat fractures and skin splits are produced by heat acting on a body whether it was alive or dead.

questions.s: A man is struck on the head with an iron rod. Skull X-ray shows a fracture of the parietal bone, but the fractured bone is not displaced and the dura is intact. Under the hurt provisions of the Pakistan Penal Code, how is this head injury classified?
questions.e: Shajjah covers hurt to the head or face. Shajjah-i-hashimah fractures the skull bone without dislocating it, which fits this undisplaced fracture. Shajjah-i-mudihah exposes the bone without fracturing it, khafifah does not expose bone, and munaqqilah involves fracture with dislocation of the bone.

questions.s: During an autopsy the doctor notes that rigor mortis is developing. In which group of voluntary muscles does rigor mortis usually appear first?
questions.e: Rigor mortis usually appears first in the small muscles around the eyelids and face, then spreads to the neck, trunk, upper limbs and lower limbs, and passes off in the same order. Among all muscles, the myocardium stiffens earliest, but the eyelids are the first voluntary muscles to show it. Small muscles of the hands and feet stiffen later.

questions.s: A body is recovered from a canal in Punjab. The right hand is tightly clenched around weeds and mud from the canal bed, and the grip cannot be loosened without force. The rest of the body is flaccid. What is this phenomenon?
questions.e: Cadaveric spasm is instantaneous rigidity of a group of muscles at the moment of death, preserving the last voluntary act, and weeds tightly grasped from the water show the person was alive when submerged. It cannot be produced after death. Rigor mortis develops gradually over hours and involves all muscles, while the rest of this body is flaccid.

questions.s: A family of four is found dead one winter morning in a closed room in Quetta with a gas heater left burning overnight. The postmortem lividity in all of them is a bright cherry-red colour. What is the most likely cause of death?
questions.e: A heater burning in a closed room produces carbon monoxide, which binds haemoglobin to form cherry-red carboxyhaemoglobin, colouring the lividity and tissues. Cyanide can give a similar colour but there is no source here, and hypothermia gives a pink colour from oxygenated blood in the cold. Aluminium phosphide is ingested, not produced by heaters.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man is found suspended from a ceiling fan by a rope. The ligature mark is above the thyroid cartilage, runs obliquely upward towards the back of the left ear, and is absent at the knot. There is a dried stream of saliva from the angle of the mouth onto the chest. What is the most likely conclusion?
questions.e: A high, oblique, non-continuous ligature mark that is interrupted at the knot is typical of hanging, and a dribble of saliva running vertically from the mouth is a sign that the person was alive when suspended. Ligature strangulation leaves a horizontal, continuous mark low on the neck, and throttling leaves fingertip bruises and nail marks rather than a ligature mark.

questions.s: A young woman's body shows small round bruises on both sides of the neck and several crescent-shaped abrasions. At autopsy there are haemorrhages in the neck muscles, a fracture of the greater horn of the hyoid bone and petechial haemorrhages in the eyes. There is no ligature mark. What is the most likely cause of death?
questions.e: Fingertip bruises and crescentic fingernail abrasions on the neck, deep muscle haemorrhage and a fractured hyoid without a ligature mark are classic of throttling (manual strangulation). Smothering affects the nose and mouth, and hanging or ligature strangulation leave a groove from the ligature.

questions.s: A body is recovered from the river Ravi. The police want to know whether the man was alive when he entered the water or was killed and thrown in. Which laboratory finding best supports death by drowning?
o: Diatoms in the femoral bone marrow
questions.e: Diatoms from the water enter the circulation through the lungs only while the heart is beating, so finding them in bone marrow or other distant organs supports antemortem drowning. Water can enter the stomach passively after death, and wrinkled 'washerwoman' skin and mud on clothes show only that the body lay in water.

questions.s: A body found indoors in Karachi in summer shows a greenish discolouration of the skin of the right lower abdomen. The rest of the skin looks unchanged. What is this finding?
questions.e: Putrefaction usually first shows as greenish discolouration over the right iliac fossa, where the caecum lies close to the skin and gut bacteria form sulphhaemoglobin. Lividity is purplish and in dependent areas, adipocere takes weeks to months to form in damp conditions, and a bruise would not be green so soon after death.

questions.s: A skeleton is found in a dry well. The forensic expert examines the pelvis to decide the sex. Which finding most strongly suggests the skeleton is female?
questions.e: The female pelvis is adapted for childbirth, with a wide greater sciatic notch, a wide subpubic angle of about 90° or more, a round inlet and often a preauricular sulcus. A narrow sciatic notch, a narrow subpubic angle and a heart-shaped inlet are male features. The pelvis is the most reliable bone for sexing an adult skeleton.

questions.s: A child's body is found and the age must be estimated. All 20 temporary teeth are present, and the four first permanent molars have just erupted behind them. No permanent incisors have erupted yet. What is the most likely age?
questions.e: The first permanent molars are the first permanent teeth to erupt, at about 6 years, behind the full set of 20 temporary teeth, which is complete by about 2 to 2½ years. Permanent central incisors begin to erupt at about 6 to 8 years, and by 9 years several temporary teeth would have been replaced.

questions.s: The fingerprints of an unidentified body are taken for comparison with the national identity database. Which fingerprint pattern is the most common in the general population?
questions.e: Loops are the most common fingerprint pattern, forming roughly two thirds of patterns, followed by whorls, with arches the least common of the main types. Fingerprint ridge patterns are formed before birth, stay the same throughout life and differ even between identical twins.

questions.s: An adult's skull is recovered, and the forensic odontologist estimates age using changes in the teeth such as attrition, secondary dentine, root resorption and root transparency. Which method is this?
questions.e: Gustafson method estimates adult age from regressive changes in a sectioned tooth, including attrition, periodontosis, secondary dentine, cementum apposition, root resorption and root transparency. The Galton system classifies fingerprints, Karl Pearson formula estimates stature from long bones, and Locard principle states that every contact leaves a trace.

questions.s: Only the lower limb bones of a body are recovered after a flood. To estimate the person's height from a single long bone using a regression formula, which bone gives the most reliable estimate?
questions.e: Stature is estimated from long bones with regression formulas such as Karl Pearson's, and the femur, the longest bone, gives the most reliable single-bone estimate, with the tibia also useful. The patella and calcaneus are short bones that correlate poorly with height, and the fibula is less reliable than the femur.

questions.s: After a bus fire on the motorway, several bodies are charred beyond recognition and relatives are waiting to claim them. Which sample is most suitable for DNA identification?
questions.e: Teeth and dense bone protect DNA from heat and decay, so a molar tooth (dental pulp) is a good source in charred remains. Hair shafts without roots contain little nuclear DNA, burnt skin is degraded by heat, and urine contains few nucleated cells.

questions.s: A woman reports sexual assault 10 hours ago. Vaginal swabs are taken, but microscopy shows no spermatozoa. The accused is known to have had a vasectomy. Which laboratory test on the swab would best confirm the presence of seminal fluid?
questions.e: Prostate-specific antigen (p30) is produced by the prostate and is present in seminal fluid even when there are no sperm, as after vasectomy or in azoospermia, so it confirms semen. Benzidine and haemin crystal tests detect blood, and the precipitin test determines whether a stain is of human or animal origin.

questions.s: A 24-year-old woman is brought by a female relative to a district hospital, saying she was sexually assaulted yesterday. The police have not yet been informed. She is distressed but medically stable. What is the most appropriate first step before examination?
o: Wait until the police bring a court order
Ask her to bathe and change first
questions.e: Medicolegal examination of a survivor of sexual assault is done only with her informed consent, explaining its purpose, with a female attendant present; treatment and evidence collection should not be delayed waiting for the police. Bathing destroys evidence, and the two-finger test has no scientific value and should not be performed.

questions.s: A 20-year-old woman is examined 36 hours after a sexual assault. Samples are collected and she is offered treatment. Her menstrual period was 12 days ago and she uses no contraception. Which additional treatment should be offered now?
questions.e: She is mid-cycle and presents within the time window, so emergency contraception (for example levonorgestrel, or a copper IUD) should be offered alongside HIV post-exposure prophylaxis assessment, hepatitis B vaccination and screening for sexually transmitted infections. Waiting 4 weeks for a test misses the chance to prevent pregnancy.

questions.s: A doctor collects vaginal swabs from a survivor of sexual assault for later laboratory examination. How should these swabs be preserved before sending them to the forensic laboratory?
o: Wrapped wet in a plastic bag
questions.e: Swabs should be air-dried at room temperature away from sunlight, then sealed, labelled and handed over with a documented chain of custody. Moisture and plastic encourage bacterial and fungal growth that destroys DNA and seminal markers, and formalin damages DNA.

questions.s: A woman is examined 12 hours after an alleged sexual assault. There are no genital injuries. Which finding provides the strongest evidence of recent vaginal intercourse?
questions.e: Finding spermatozoa in vaginal swabs is the most definite evidence of recent intercourse, and DNA from them can identify the assailant. Vulval redness and discharge are non-specific, and the state of the hymen is a poor guide because it varies naturally and may stretch without tearing.

questions.s: A 30-year-old farmer from a cotton-growing area of southern Punjab is brought after drinking a pesticide. He has pinpoint pupils, profuse sweating and salivation, crackles in both lungs, muscle twitching and a pulse of 48/min. What is the most important drug to give first?
questions.e: Miosis, secretions, bronchorrhoea, bradycardia and fasciculations are the cholinergic crisis of organophosphate poisoning, and atropine given in rapidly increasing doses until the chest is clear and the heart rate is adequate is the life-saving first drug. Naloxone reverses opioids, which do not cause sweating or fasciculations, and physostigmine would worsen cholinergic toxicity.

questions.s: A 19-year-old woman swallowed tablets kept to protect stored wheat from insects. She has vomiting, a garlic-like smell on her breath, and severe hypotension that does not respond to fluids. Which toxic agent is responsible for her poisoning?
questions.e: Wheat pills contain aluminium phosphide, which releases phosphine gas on contact with stomach acid; phosphine blocks mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase and causes profound refractory shock and myocardial damage. There is no specific antidote, so treatment is supportive. The garlic smell and refractory shock distinguish it from organophosphate poisoning.

questions.s: A train passenger is brought unconscious to a hospital in Rohri after accepting sweets from a stranger; his wallet is missing. He has hot dry flushed skin, dilated pupils, a pulse of 130/min, a distended bladder and mutters incoherently. Which poison is most likely?
questions.e: Datura seeds contain atropine-like alkaloids, giving the anticholinergic picture of dry hot skin, dilated pupils, tachycardia, urinary retention and delirium, and they have been used to drug travellers for robbery. Opium causes pinpoint pupils and slow breathing, and organophosphates cause the opposite, cholinergic, picture.

questions.s: A 12-year-old boy sleeping on the floor of a mud house in rural Sindh woke at night with abdominal pain. In the morning he has drooping eyelids, double vision and difficulty swallowing. There is no pain or swelling anywhere, only two tiny marks on the hand. A 20-minute whole blood clotting test shows normal clotting. Which snake most likely bit him?
questions.e: A painless bite at night in someone sleeping on the floor, with abdominal pain, ptosis and progressive paralysis but no local swelling and normal clotting, is typical of the common krait, whose venom is neurotoxic. Vipers cause painful local swelling and non-clotting blood, and cobra bites usually cause marked local pain, swelling and necrosis.

questions.s: A 40-year-old farmer was bitten on the foot while cutting grass in Thar 4 hours ago. The foot is painfully swollen to the knee and his gums are bleeding. A 20-minute whole blood clotting test shows the blood has not clotted. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Incision and suction of the bite
questions.e: Local swelling with bleeding gums and an unclotted 20-minute whole blood clotting test indicate viper envenomation with venom-induced coagulopathy, which is an indication for polyvalent anti-snake venom. Tourniquets and incision are harmful first aid. Blood products alone do not neutralise the venom, which keeps consuming clotting factors.

questions.s: Several adults in a village where families drink water from a deep hand pump have dark raindrop-like spots on the trunk with pale spots between them and thickened, warty skin on the palms and soles. One has white transverse bands across the fingernails. Which poisoning is most likely?
questions.e: Raindrop pigmentation, palmar and plantar hyperkeratosis and Mees lines on the nails are characteristic of chronic arsenic poisoning, which in parts of Pakistan comes from contaminated groundwater. Lead causes a blue gum line, anaemia and neuropathy, mercury causes tremor and gingivitis, and fluorosis causes mottled teeth and skeletal changes.

questions.s: Three men are brought to an emergency room in Karachi 24 hours after drinking illicit home-made liquor at a wedding. All have blurred vision, abdominal pain and rapid deep breathing. Blood gas shows pH 7.05 with a high anion gap. Which treatment specifically blocks formation of the toxic metabolite?
questions.e: Visual blurring and high anion gap acidosis after illicit liquor indicate methanol poisoning; alcohol dehydrogenase converts methanol to formic acid, which damages the optic nerve. Fomepizole, or ethanol if it is unavailable, competitively blocks alcohol dehydrogenase. Bicarbonate corrects acidosis but does not stop metabolism, and haemodialysis removes methanol and formate.

questions.s: A 22-year-old woman drank a black hair dye (kala pathar) dissolved in water 3 hours ago after a family dispute. Her face, lips, tongue and neck are massively swollen, she has stridor, and her urine is dark brown. Which complication is the most immediate threat to her life?
questions.e: Paraphenylenediamine hair dye causes rapid, severe cervicofacial and laryngeal oedema, and upper airway obstruction is the most immediate cause of death, often needing tracheostomy. It also causes rhabdomyolysis, giving dark urine, and later acute kidney injury, which is important but less immediate than the airway.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man with extensive burns after a kerosene fire is expected to die. The police ask the medical officer to have his dying declaration recorded. What is the most important role of the doctor?
o: Record the statement in his own words
Certify the patient is mentally fit to speak
Witness the signature of the patient
Ask leading questions to speed it up
questions.e: A dying declaration is preferably recorded by a magistrate, and the doctor's key role is to certify that the patient is conscious, oriented and mentally fit (compos mentis) to make the statement, before and after it is recorded. If no magistrate is available a doctor may record it in the patient's own words, without leading questions.

questions.s: A doctor is called as a witness in a criminal trial in a sessions court and is asked about the HIV status of a patient he treated. He objects that this is confidential. The judge directs him to answer. What should the doctor do?
o: Answer only if the patient is present
Leave the court and inform the PM&DC
questions.e: Confidentiality is a strong duty but not absolute: a doctor may ask the court to respect it, but when a judge directs him to answer he must comply, and the disclosure is limited to what is asked. Refusing would be contempt of court. Other recognised exceptions include notifiable diseases and serious risk to others.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman develops chronic abdominal pain after a caesarean section. An X-ray 6 months later shows a surgical swab with a radio-opaque marker in her abdomen. In a negligence claim, which legal principle allows the facts to speak for themselves without expert evidence?
questions.e: Res ipsa loquitur ('the thing speaks for itself') applies when the injury would not ordinarily happen without negligence and the cause was under the defendant's control, as with a swab left in the abdomen, so the burden shifts to the doctor. The Bolam test judges the standard of care against a responsible body of medical opinion.

questions.s: An unconscious young man is brought to the emergency room after a road traffic accident with a rapidly expanding extradural haematoma. No relative or guardian can be found. What is the legal basis for performing emergency surgery?
o: Written consent from the police officer
Treatment must wait for a relative
questions.e: In a life-threatening emergency when the patient cannot consent and no guardian is available, the doctor may give necessary treatment under the doctrine of necessity, also called implied consent. Police officers and administrators cannot consent on the patient's behalf, and waiting for a relative would risk the patient's life.

questions.s: A body with injuries is found beside a canal in a district of Punjab. Before the body is sent for postmortem examination, an inquiry into the apparent cause of death is held and a report prepared. In Pakistan, which type of inquest is most commonly held in such cases?
questions.e: In Pakistan the police inquest under the Code of Criminal Procedure is the usual type: the police officer inspects the body, prepares the inquest report and sends it for postmortem examination. Magistrate inquests are held in special situations such as deaths in custody, and coroner and medical examiner systems are not used in Pakistan.

questions.s: A patient sues a surgeon after a known complication occurs. Several expert surgeons testify that they would have used the same technique, which is accepted by a responsible body of surgical opinion, though other surgeons prefer a different method. Which legal test is used to decide whether the surgeon met the standard of care?
questions.e: The Bolam test holds that a doctor is not negligent if he acted in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical opinion, even if other doctors would act differently. Res ipsa loquitur applies to obvious errors, and the M'Naghten rule concerns criminal responsibility in insanity.

questions.s: A man was hit once on the forehead with a stick 2 days ago. He now has bruising around the left eye, although the eye and eyelids were not struck. There is no fracture. What best explains the bruise around the eye?
o: A second blow to the eye
Fracture of the base of skull
questions.e: Blood from a bruise can track along tissue planes under gravity and appear at a distance from the site of impact, so a blow to the forehead can produce a black eye a day or two later. This is why the site of a bruise does not always mark the point of impact. A skull base fracture causes bilateral periorbital bruising with other signs, and no fracture is present here.

questions.s: A man has a wound on the abdomen with clean-cut margins. The skin opening is 2 cm long, but the track passes 10 cm deep into the peritoneal cavity. One end of the wound is sharp and the other blunt. What type of wound is this?
questions.e: A stab wound is made by a pointed weapon driven in, so its depth exceeds its length; a sharp and a blunt end suggest a single-edged knife. An incised wound is longer than it is deep, a laceration has irregular, bruised margins, and a chop wound is made by a heavy edged weapon and is wide and deep.

questions.s: In a land dispute a man was attacked with a heavy, sharp-edged gandasa. He has a gaping wound on the shoulder with fairly clean margins, slightly bruised edges, and the underlying bone is deeply cut. How should this wound be classified?
questions.e: A heavy weapon with a sharp edge, such as a gandasa, axe or sword, produces a chop wound: deep, gaping, with sharp but slightly bruised margins and cuts or fractures of underlying bone. A simple incised wound from a light blade is superficial and does not cut bone. A stab wound is narrow and deeper than it is long.

questions.s: At autopsy of a man shot once, the doctor finds two wounds. One on the back is larger, irregular and slit-like with everted edges, and has no abrasion collar, blackening or tattooing. What is this wound most likely to be?
questions.e: An exit wound is usually larger and irregular, with everted edges and no abrasion collar or powder marks, because the bullet is deformed and tumbling and pushes tissue outward. Entry wounds are usually smaller with inverted edges and an abrasion collar, with blackening or tattooing at close range.

questions.s: A man is found dead with a firearm wound on the right temple. The wound is star-shaped with ragged tears, there is a circular imprint of the muzzle on the surrounding skin, and the tissues deep in the wound track are cherry-red. There is little powder tattooing on the skin around it. What is the range of fire?
questions.e: In a contact shot over bone, gases expand under the skin and tear it into a stellate wound, the recoiling skin stamps a muzzle imprint, and carbon monoxide in the gases makes the track cherry-red. Because the muzzle touches the skin, smoke and powder go into the wound rather than tattooing the surrounding skin, unlike a close-range shot.

questions.s: A man has been shot with a shotgun. There are multiple small round pellet wounds scattered over his back with no single central hole. Which feature is mainly used to estimate how far away the gun was fired?
questions.e: Shotgun pellets leave the barrel together and spread out with distance, so the diameter of the pellet pattern is the main guide to range, ideally compared with test firing of the same weapon. At very close range the pellets enter as a single hole. The size of individual pellet holes depends mostly on the shot size, not the distance.

questions.s: A farmer is found dead in an open field after a thunderstorm in Swat. His clothes are torn and singed, his metal belt buckle is fused, and there are red, branching, fern-like marks on his chest and shoulders. What are these skin marks called?
questions.e: Fern-like, branching red marks on the skin (arborescent or Lichtenberg figures) are characteristic of lightning strike and fade within hours, so they may be absent at autopsy. Joule burns are small crater-like marks at the contact point of an electric current, and Tardieu spots are petechial haemorrhages seen in asphyxia.

questions.s: An electrician died while repairing a live wire at home. On his right index finger there is a small, round, greyish-white crater with a raised, pale rim and no surrounding redness. What is this lesion?
questions.e: A Joule burn is a small, round, pale crater with a raised rim at the point where electric current entered the body, formed by heat generated as current passes through skin resistance. Its pale colour and shape distinguish it from an abrasion or a blister. A search for it on the hands is important because low-voltage electrocution may leave no other sign.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman has burns involving the whole of her right upper limb and the whole front of her trunk after a stove burst. Using the rule of nines, approximately what percentage of the body surface is burnt?
questions.e: In the adult rule of nines each upper limb is 9 % and the front of the trunk is 18 %, giving 27 %. The extent of burns guides fluid resuscitation and, in medicolegal work, prognosis and assessment of the case. Stove burst and kerosene burns are a frequent cause of burns in women in Pakistan and must be documented carefully.

questions.s: At autopsy of a body pulled from a river, the doctor must decide whether a deep cut on the arm was made before or after death. Which finding best indicates the wound was made during life?
o: Wound edges are pale and closely applied
Wound found in a dependent part of the body
Gaping edges with blood infiltrating the tissues
questions.e: Wounds made during life show vital reactions: the edges gape because of muscle and skin tone, blood clots in the wound and infiltrates the surrounding tissues, and later inflammation develops. Postmortem wounds do not gape much, have pale edges and no infiltration or clotting. Wounds in dependent areas may ooze after death, so position alone is misleading.

questions.s: A young man was hit on the side of the head with a cricket ball, was briefly knocked out, then walked home talking normally. Four hours later he became drowsy with a dilated left pupil. CT shows a lens-shaped haematoma under a temporal bone fracture. Which vessel is most likely torn?
questions.e: A temporal bone fracture tearing the middle meningeal artery causes an extradural haematoma, which is biconvex on CT and often follows a lucid interval before rapid deterioration. Torn bridging veins cause a crescent-shaped subdural haematoma, and the middle cerebral artery lies inside the brain's coverings.

questions.s: A man was stabbed in the abdomen and the knife entered the peritoneal cavity, though no internal organ was injured. Under the hurt provisions of the Pakistan Penal Code, what is an injury that extends into the body cavity of the trunk called?
questions.e: Jaifah is hurt in which the injury extends to the body cavity of the trunk, whether or not an organ is injured. Ghayr-jaifah covers wounds that do not enter a body cavity, shajjah-i-ammah is a head injury reaching the membranes of the brain, and itlaf-i-udw means dismemberment or loss of a limb or organ.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man on a ventilator after a severe head injury is being assessed for brainstem death. Preconditions have been met and reversible causes excluded. Which finding is compatible with a diagnosis of brainstem death?
o: Breathing effort during the apnoea test
questions.e: Brainstem death requires absent brainstem reflexes (pupillary, corneal, vestibulo-ocular, gag, cough) and no respiratory effort on apnoea testing, but spinal reflexes such as tendon jerks can persist because they do not depend on the brainstem. Any pupillary response, gag or breathing effort means the brainstem is still functioning.

questions.s: A body found lying on its back in a field has fixed purple postmortem lividity over the front of the chest and face, with pale areas over the nose and chest that do not change when pressed. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Bruising from a beating before death
Death from drowning in a canal
Body moved after lividity became fixed
questions.e: Lividity develops in dependent parts and becomes fixed after several hours, so fixed lividity on the front of a body found lying on its back means it lay face down for hours after death and was then moved. Lividity is uniform and lies in dependent areas, unlike bruises, and carbon monoxide changes its colour, not its position.

questions.s: A body is recovered from a waterlogged grave months after burial. The fat of the cheeks, buttocks and thighs has turned into a greyish-white, waxy, greasy material with a rancid smell. What is this change called?
questions.e: Adipocere forms when body fat is hydrolysed and hydrogenated into waxy fatty acids in moist, warm, airless conditions such as water or wet graves, over weeks to months, and it preserves features and injuries. Mummification is drying in hot, dry air, maceration affects a fetus dead in utero, and marbling is an early sign of putrefaction.

questions.s: A shepherd's body is found months after he went missing in the hot, dry sand of the Cholistan desert. The skin is dry, leathery and brown, closely stretched over the bones, and the body is light and odourless. What is this change called?
questions.e: Mummification is the drying and shrivelling of tissues in hot, dry, airy conditions such as desert sand, leaving leathery brown skin over the bones and preserving features for identification. Adipocere needs moisture, putrefaction produces bloating and smell, and maceration is the change in a fetus dying in the uterus.

questions.s: A patient dies in a hospital ward. One hour later the body temperature is found to be higher than it was at the time of death. In which condition is this postmortem rise in temperature most likely?
questions.e: Postmortem caloricity is a rise in body temperature in the first hours after death, seen when heat production was very high before death or continues from bacterial activity, as in septicaemia, cholera, tetanus, strychnine poisoning and heatstroke. Haemorrhage, hypothermia and sedative overdose are associated with low body temperature.

questions.s: A body is recovered from a burnt house with the elbows, wrists, knees and hips flexed and the fists clenched, like a boxer's guard. What causes this posture?
o: Cadaveric spasm at the moment of death
Rigor mortis in a cold room
questions.e: The pugilistic attitude results from heat coagulating and shortening muscle proteins, and because flexors are bulkier than extensors the limbs flex. It occurs whether the person was alive or dead when burnt, so it does not indicate antemortem burning or a struggle. Cadaveric spasm affects only a group of muscles and occurs at the moment of death.

questions.s: A body recovered from a canal after several hours shows white, wrinkled, sodden skin on the palms and soles. What does this finding indicate?
o: Person was alive on entering water
Body was in water for some time
Death occurred more than a week ago
questions.e: Washerwoman's skin forms in both living and dead bodies after prolonged immersion as the thick skin of the palms and soles absorbs water, so it shows only that the body was in water for some hours. It does not prove drowning or that the person was alive when entering the water. Diatoms in distant organs and fine persistent froth are more specific for drowning.

questions.s: A man was crushed against a wall by a crowd at a religious gathering. At autopsy the face, neck and upper chest are deeply congested and purple with numerous petechiae and subconjunctival haemorrhages, sharply demarcated at the level of the chest. There are no neck injuries. What is the most likely cause of death?
questions.e: Compression of the chest and upper abdomen prevents breathing and forces venous blood back into the head and neck, giving intense congestion, petechiae and subconjunctival haemorrhages above the compression level: traumatic (crush) asphyxia, seen in stampedes. Throttling and hanging leave neck marks, and smothering leaves marks around the nose and mouth.

questions.s: A forensic expert wants to estimate the time since death in a body found 2 days after death in a cool room. Which body fluid shows a steady rise in potassium concentration after death that can be used for this purpose?
questions.e: Potassium leaks from cells of the retina and lens into the vitreous humour at a fairly steady rate after death, so vitreous potassium is used to help estimate the postmortem interval. The vitreous is protected within the eye from contamination and early putrefaction, which makes it more reliable than blood or CSF.

questions.s: A newborn baby delivered at home appears lifeless with no detectable pulse or breathing. After 10 minutes of resuscitation by the lady health worker, the baby starts breathing. What was this state of apparent death?
questions.e: Suspended animation is a state in which vital functions are depressed to a level so low that they cannot be detected clinically, yet life persists and resuscitation can succeed; it is seen in newborns, drowning, electrocution and hypothermia. Somatic and brainstem death are irreversible, and molecular death is the later death of individual cells.

questions.s: A skull is found in a field. It is large and rugged, with prominent supraorbital ridges, a sloping forehead, large mastoid processes and a square chin. What is the most likely sex?
o: Cannot be judged from a skull
questions.e: Prominent brow ridges, a sloping forehead, large mastoid processes, marked muscle markings and a square chin are typical of an adult male skull; females have a smoother skull, a vertical forehead and smaller mastoids. The skull is second only to the pelvis for sexing, and prepubertal skulls show few differences.

questions.s: A girl brought to court claims to be 15 years old, but no birth record is available. The court asks a medical board to estimate her age. Which method is most appropriate for a living teenager?
o: Gustafson method on an extracted tooth
X-rays to assess ossification and fusion
questions.e: In living children and young adults, age is estimated mainly from X-rays of joints such as the elbow, wrist, shoulder and pelvis, which show the appearance and fusion of ossification centres, together with dental eruption and physical development. Gustafson method needs a sectioned tooth, skull suture closure is unreliable and late, and height and weight vary widely.

questions.s: An unidentified young adult body is examined. All second permanent molars have erupted, and the third molars have also erupted in all four quadrants. Approximately which age range does eruption of the third molars suggest?
questions.e: Third molars usually erupt between about 17 and 25 years, while second molars erupt at about 12 to 13 years, so erupted third molars suggest at least late adolescence. Their timing is variable and some never erupt, so they are used together with other age indicators.

questions.s: Police suspect one of two identical twin brothers of a burglary. DNA profiling of blood found at the scene matches both brothers equally. Which identification method can distinguish between them?
questions.e: Monozygotic twins share the same nuclear and mitochondrial DNA, blood group and HLA type, but their fingerprints differ because ridge details are shaped by local conditions in the womb. Fingerprints at the scene can therefore separate them. Every person's fingerprint ridge detail is unique and unchanged through life.

questions.s: Only a small partial fingerprint is recovered from a glass at a crime scene, too small to show enough ridge characteristics for routine comparison. The expert instead compares the size, shape and arrangement of the sweat pore openings along the ridges. What is this technique called?
questions.e: Poroscopy, introduced by Locard, identifies a person from the number, shape and position of sweat pores on the ridges, which is useful when only a fragment of print is available. Dactylography is the study of ridge patterns in general, rugoscopy uses palatal rugae, and cheiloscopy uses lip prints.

questions.s: A forensic team collects fibres from a victim's clothing that match the suspect's shawl, and soil from the suspect's shoes that matches the crime scene. Which principle underlies collecting this trace evidence?
questions.e: Locard exchange principle states that every contact leaves a trace: a person at a scene both leaves material there and carries material away, which is the basis for collecting fibres, soil, hair and similar trace evidence. Galton is linked with fingerprint classification and Nysten law describes the order in which rigor mortis appears.

questions.s: A skull is found buried in a field. Police have photographs of a man missing for 2 years. The forensic expert overlays a photograph of the skull, taken at the same angle and scale, on the man's portrait to compare outlines and landmarks. What is this technique?
questions.e: Superimposition overlays an image of the skull on a photograph of the missing person, matching the outline, orbits, nasal opening and teeth; it is better at excluding than proving identity. Facial reconstruction builds soft tissue on the skull without a photograph, and the cephalic index is a skull shape measurement.

questions.s: Fragments of tissue are recovered after an explosion, and the sex of the person must be determined. Microscopy of cell nuclei shows a small dark chromatin mass on the inner nuclear membrane in many cells. What does this indicate?
questions.e: The Barr body is an inactivated X chromosome seen as a dense chromatin mass against the nuclear membrane; it is present in cells with two X chromosomes and so indicates a female. Male cells, with one X chromosome, lack it. DNA testing for Y-chromosome markers is now more reliable but the principle remains a common question.

questions.s: A glass at a crime scene shows a clear print of the grooves and wrinkles of a person's lips. The pattern is compared with a suspect's lip print. What is this method of identification called?
questions.e: Cheiloscopy is the study of lip prints, whose groove patterns are thought to be individual and stable. Rugoscopy studies the ridges of the hard palate, poroscopy the sweat pores of fingerprints, and forensic odontology the teeth and bite marks.

questions.s: A 19-year-old woman phones a hospital helpline 6 hours after a sexual assault. She wants to come for help but asks whether she can bathe and change first. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Bathe and wash the clothes before coming
Avoid bathing and bring the clothes
Wait a week until she feels calmer
Douche the vagina to prevent infection
questions.e: Survivors should, if they can, come without bathing, douching or changing, and bring the clothes worn during the assault in a paper bag, because these hold semen, hair, fibres and DNA. She should be seen as early as possible for evidence collection, emergency contraception and HIV prophylaxis, though she can still be examined if she has bathed.

questions.s: A 25-year-old woman is examined 30 hours after a sexual assault by an unknown man. She is worried about HIV. What is the time limit within which HIV post-exposure prophylaxis should be started?
o: Only after a positive HIV test
questions.e: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis should start as soon as possible and within 72 hours of exposure, after a baseline HIV test, and continues for 28 days. Waiting for her to test positive defeats the purpose, and starting after 72 hours is not recommended because benefit is unlikely.

questions.s: A man accused of sexual assault is brought by the police for medical examination with a magistrate's order. Which sample is most useful for comparing his DNA profile with evidence from the victim?
questions.e: A buccal swab or blood sample gives a reliable reference DNA profile from the accused for comparison with DNA from the victim's swabs. Cut hair lacks roots and so has little nuclear DNA, and urine contains few cells. Penile swabs may also be taken to look for the victim's cells.

questions.s: An 8-year-old girl is brought to a paediatric clinic with a purulent vaginal discharge. Culture grows Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Her mother says nothing unusual has happened. What is the most appropriate step besides treating the infection?
o: Reassure as it was caught from a towel
Treat the mother as the source
questions.e: Gonorrhoea beyond the newborn period is almost always sexually transmitted, so in a prepubertal child it is a strong indicator of sexual abuse and must lead to a child protection assessment and appropriate reporting. Non-sexual spread from towels is not an acceptable explanation, and the child must be kept safe while this is investigated.

questions.s: A doctor examines a 30-year-old married woman 2 days after she reports rape. She has no genital or body injuries, and swab results are awaited. Which statement is most appropriate in the medicolegal report?
o: Rape did not occur as there are no injuries
Absence of injury does not exclude assault
questions.e: Many sexual assaults leave no physical injury, especially in adult women and when examination is delayed, so the report should state that absence of injury neither confirms nor excludes assault, and give a final opinion after laboratory results. Comments on a woman's sexual history or the truth of her allegation are outside the doctor's role and are inappropriate.

questions.s: The clothing of a sexual assault survivor is damp and stained. How should it be packed before handing it to the police for laboratory examination?
o: All items together in one plastic bag
Washed gently to remove mud first
Folded wet into a sealed plastic box
Air-dried, each item in a separate paper bag
questions.e: Stained clothing should be air-dried at room temperature and each item packed separately in a labelled, sealed paper bag, with chain of custody recorded. Plastic traps moisture and promotes bacterial growth that degrades DNA, packing items together causes cross-contamination, and washing destroys evidence.

questions.s: A woman reports being sexually assaulted 4 days ago. She has not bathed thoroughly since. The duty medical officer says that after 72 hours no samples are worth collecting. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Send her home, as evidence is lost
Collect only a urine pregnancy test
questions.e: Spermatozoa and DNA can sometimes be detected in the vagina and cervix several days after intercourse, and injuries may still be visible, so examination and swabs should be done even after 72 hours. The examination also allows treatment, emergency contraception (a copper IUD can still be used within 5 days), and documentation.

questions.s: A farmer with organophosphate poisoning is given atropine. The doctor also considers pralidoxime. Why should pralidoxime, if used, be started early?
o: It is only absorbed in the first hour
It cannot reactivate the enzyme after ageing
It reverses the effect of atropine later
questions.e: Pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase by removing the organophosphate from the enzyme, but over time the bound enzyme undergoes 'ageing', after which it cannot be reactivated. Atropine is the essential first drug because it blocks muscarinic effects, while oximes work only before ageing and their benefit is debated.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man with organophosphate poisoning is receiving repeated IV atropine. Which finding is the main target showing adequate atropinisation?
questions.e: Atropine is titrated against secretions and haemodynamics: the targets are a clear chest with no bronchorrhoea, heart rate above about 80/min, systolic pressure above 80 mmHg and dry axillae. Pupil size is unreliable, and a heart rate above 140, absent bowel sounds or confusion suggest atropine toxicity.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy drank from a soft drink bottle containing kerosene oil 30 minutes ago. He coughed and choked at the time and is now breathing fast. What should be avoided?
questions.e: The main danger of kerosene ingestion is aspiration pneumonitis, and inducing vomiting or doing gastric lavage greatly increases the risk of aspiration, so both are avoided. Management is observation, oxygen if needed and a chest X-ray if respiratory signs persist. Storing kerosene in drink bottles is a common cause in Pakistan.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman swallowed toilet-cleaning acid an hour ago. She has burns on the lips, drooling and pain on swallowing, but her airway is clear and she is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Nil by mouth and early endoscopy
Gastric lavage with a large tube
questions.e: After corrosive ingestion the airway is assessed first; then the patient is kept nil by mouth with IV fluids and analgesia, and endoscopy within the first day grades the injury. Emesis and lavage re-expose the oesophagus and risk perforation, and neutralising agents generate heat that worsens injury.

questions.s: A 17-year-old girl took a large number of paracetamol tablets 6 hours ago after an argument. She is well apart from nausea. The plasma paracetamol level is well above the treatment line on the nomogram. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Observe and repeat the level at 24 hours
questions.e: A paracetamol level above the treatment line requires IV N-acetylcysteine, which replenishes glutathione and prevents liver damage, and is most effective within 8 to 10 hours of ingestion. Activated charcoal helps only within about an hour. Feeling well early is typical, as liver injury appears after 24 to 72 hours.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman is brought in drowsy with headache and vomiting after sleeping in a room with a coal-burning angithi. Her oxygen saturation reads 98 % on pulse oximetry. Carboxyhaemoglobin is 25 %. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
o: Oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula
No oxygen as saturation is normal
questions.e: Carbon monoxide poisoning is treated with high-flow 100 % oxygen through a tight-fitting non-rebreathing mask, which shortens the half-life of carboxyhaemoglobin, with hyperbaric oxygen considered in severe cases. Pulse oximeters read carboxyhaemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin, so a normal reading is falsely reassuring. Nitrites are used for cyanide.

questions.s: A 45-year-old jewellery worker collapses after accidentally drinking an electroplating solution. He has seizures, severe lactic acidosis and a smell of bitter almonds on his breath. Venous blood looks bright red. Which antidote is most appropriate?
questions.e: Electroplating and jewellery work use cyanide salts; cyanide blocks cytochrome oxidase so tissues cannot use oxygen, giving lactic acidosis and bright red venous blood, sometimes with a bitter almond smell. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, which is excreted in urine. Desferrioxamine treats iron poisoning.

questions.s: A 40-year-old worker at a battery recycling unit has colicky abdominal pain, constipation and weakness of wrist extension. There is a bluish line along the gum margins. Hb is 9.8 g/dL. What finding on the blood film is most typical?
questions.e: Lead inhibits enzymes of haem synthesis and pyrimidine nucleotidase, causing anaemia with basophilic stippling of red cells, along with abdominal colic, wrist drop and a blue gum (Burton) line. Target cells suggest thalassaemia or liver disease, Howell–Jolly bodies hyposplenism, and schistocytes haemolysis from red cell fragmentation.

questions.s: A 23-year-old man is found unresponsive in a park in Peshawar with a syringe beside him. Respiratory rate is 6/min and his pupils are pinpoint. What is the most appropriate drug to give?
questions.e: Coma, slow breathing and pinpoint pupils in a person with a syringe indicate opioid overdose such as heroin, and naloxone reverses it rapidly while ventilation is supported. Because naloxone is short-acting, the patient must be observed for recurrent sedation. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, which do not cause pinpoint pupils.

questions.s: A 20-year-old woman ate crushed seeds of the yellow oleander plant from a roadside hedge. She has vomiting, a pulse of 38/min with second-degree heart block, and serum potassium of 6.1 mmol/L. Which specific treatment is most appropriate?
questions.e: Yellow oleander contains cardiac glycosides that act like digoxin, causing vomiting, bradyarrhythmias, heart block and hyperkalaemia, and digoxin-specific antibody fragments bind them and reverse toxicity. Calcium is traditionally avoided in glycoside toxicity, and pralidoxime is for organophosphates. Charcoal is supportive but not enough alone.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy swallowed many of his pregnant mother's iron tablets 3 hours ago. He has vomited blood-stained material and has diarrhoea, and he is becoming drowsy. Serum iron is markedly raised. Which antidote is indicated?
questions.e: Iron overdose causes vomiting, haematemesis and diarrhoea, then shock, acidosis and liver failure, and desferrioxamine chelates free iron in serious toxicity. Activated charcoal does not bind iron, and penicillamine and dimercaprol are chelators used for copper, lead, arsenic and mercury.

questions.s: A 10-year-old boy was stung by a scorpion on the foot while collecting firewood. Two hours later he is sweating, vomiting and salivating, with cold extremities, BP 170/110 mmHg and crackles at both lung bases. Which drug is most appropriate?
questions.e: Venom of dangerous scorpions causes an autonomic storm with intense alpha-adrenergic stimulation, hypertension and pulmonary oedema, and the alpha-blocker prazosin is the established treatment. Atropine worsens tachycardia and the adrenergic crisis. Diuretics alone do not address the cause of the pulmonary oedema.

questions.s: A surgeon is about to obtain consent from a 45-year-old man for elective cholecystectomy. The patient is alert and understands Urdu. For his consent to be valid, what must the surgeon explain?
questions.e: Valid informed consent requires a competent patient who gives it voluntarily after being told, in language he understands, the nature and purpose of the procedure, its material risks, the alternatives including no treatment, and the likely outcome. Explaining only benefits or logistics does not make consent informed.

questions.s: A doctor in an outpatient clinic wants to send an HIV test for a 30-year-old man with weight loss and oral thrush. The man is mentally competent. What is required before the test is sent?
questions.e: HIV testing of a competent adult requires his own informed consent, given after pre-test counselling about the test and its implications, and the result is confidential. Employers, spouses and police have no right to consent on his behalf. Partner notification is discussed with him after a positive result.

questions.s: A young man is brought to the emergency room of a THQ hospital with a bleeding stab wound to the thigh after a fight. No police officer has come with him. What should the duty doctor do first?
o: Wait for the police to arrive
Refuse care until a report is lodged
Refer him to a teaching hospital
questions.e: In a medicolegal case the doctor's first duty is to save life and treat the injury; treatment must never be delayed for police formalities. The case is then registered as a medicolegal case, injuries documented and the police informed. Refusing or delaying care, or unnecessary referral, is professional misconduct.

questions.s: A complaint reaches the medical regulatory council that a male doctor began a sexual relationship with a female patient he was treating for depression. How would this conduct be classified?
questions.e: A sexual relationship with a current patient abuses the trust and power of the doctor–patient relationship and is serious professional misconduct (infamous conduct), for which the regulatory council can suspend or remove the doctor's registration. Negligence concerns failure in the standard of care causing harm, which is a different matter.

questions.s: A staff nurse employed by a private hospital in Lahore gives a wrong injection, harming a patient. The patient sues the hospital as well as the nurse. On what legal basis is the hospital held responsible?
questions.e: Under vicarious liability an employer is responsible for the negligent acts of employees done in the course of their work, so the hospital answers for its nurse. Res ipsa loquitur is a rule of evidence for obvious negligence, the doctrine of necessity justifies emergency treatment without consent, and therapeutic privilege concerns withholding harmful information.

questions.s: A diabetic patient with a foot ulcer was told clearly, with a written record, to return in 2 days and to keep his weight off the foot. He returned after 3 weeks with gangrene and sues the doctor for not preventing amputation. Which defence is the doctor most likely to raise?
questions.e: Contributory negligence applies when the patient's own failure to follow reasonable advice contributed to the harm; here the documented instructions he ignored would reduce or defeat the claim. Res ipsa loquitur helps a claimant, not a defendant, and vicarious liability concerns an employer's responsibility for staff.

questions.s: The son of a 78-year-old man with terminal cancer asks the doctor to give his father a lethal injection to end his suffering. What is the legal position of active euthanasia in Pakistan?
o: Legal if the patient is unconscious
questions.e: Active euthanasia, deliberately ending a patient's life, is unlawful in Pakistan and would be treated as homicide whatever the family's wishes. The doctor's role is good palliative care, including adequate pain relief and symptom control, and honest discussion with the patient and family.

questions.s: A man was buried a month ago after his death was recorded as natural. His brother now alleges poisoning, and the investigation needs a postmortem examination. Who is legally empowered to order exhumation of the body?
questions.e: Exhumation of a buried body for medicolegal examination can be ordered only by a magistrate, and it is done in the magistrate's presence with the grave and body identified. Police officers, health officials and the family cannot authorise it on their own. Samples of soil around the body are taken as controls in suspected poisoning.

questions.s: A poor labourer from a village in Punjab is offered money by an agent to sell one of his kidneys to a foreign patient at a private clinic. What is the legal position in Pakistan?
o: Legal if a doctor certifies fitness
Legal if the donor agrees in writing
Legal if the recipient is foreign
questions.e: Pakistan's law on transplantation of human organs and tissues prohibits commercial dealing in organs, and buying or selling a kidney is a criminal offence for the agent, the clinic and the doctors involved. Living donation is allowed only under the law's conditions, such as from close relatives with proper approval, regardless of the donor's written agreement.

questions.s: A factory manager phones a doctor to ask whether one of his workers, who attended the clinic last week, is HIV positive. The worker has not given permission for any disclosure. What should the doctor do?
o: Disclose it, as the employer pays
Give only a hint to the manager
questions.e: Information about a patient is confidential and may not be given to an employer without the patient's consent; HIV is not spread by ordinary workplace contact, so there is no public-interest reason for disclosure. Recognised exceptions include court orders, statutory notification and serious risk to an identifiable person.
